name: Bar Ben Fiddich
nameJa: バー ベンフィディック
description: Ranked #18 on World's 50 Best Bars 2025. No printed menu -- bartender Hiroyasu Kayama crafts bespoke cocktails using herbs and botanicals grown on his family's Chichibu farm. He forages, distills, and infuses in-house. Each visit is a unique omakase cocktail experience.
howToFind: 9th floor of an unmarked building on Shinjuku's west side near the Hilton. Look for the small building entrance on a side street off Ome-Kaido -- take the elevator to the 9th floor. No sign outside.
tips: Reservations strongly recommended via TableCheck. Expect to pay 2500-4000 yen per cocktail. Seats about 12 people. Smart casual dress code.

name: SG Club
description: Three bars in one by acclaimed bartender Shingo Gokan. Guzzle (ground floor) is a casual wood-clad lounge. Sip (basement) is an industrial speakeasy with craft cocktails. Savor (upstairs) is members-only cigar lounge. Inspired by the first Japanese delegation to the US in 1860.
howToFind: Located on a side street in Shibuya, look for the ground-floor Guzzle entrance. Head downstairs for the speakeasy Sip bar in the basement. The building is near Shibuya Center-gai.
tips: Sip (basement) is the speakeasy experience -- go there for the full hidden bar vibe. Guzzle is great for a casual first drink. Cocktails run 1800-2500 yen.

name: A10
description: A record bar hidden behind a wall of coin lockers across from Ebisu Park. Pull open one of the locker boxes and the entire wall swings open to reveal stairs descending into a 1920s New York-style speakeasy filled with vintage vinyl. Live DJ plays 90s and 00s hits on a vintage sound system.
howToFind: Across from Ebisu Park, look for what appears to be a row of lockers at basement level of Bios Building. Pull open the correct locker door and the wall swings open. Address: 1-12-11 Ebisunishi, Shibuya, B1F Bios Building.
tips: 1100 yen service/cover charge. Cocktails around 1650 yen. Open 7pm-3am, closed Wednesdays. Walk-ins OK but can get crowded on weekends.
mapsQuery: A10 bar Ebisu Tokyo coin locker speakeasy

name: Gen Yamamoto
description: An omakase cocktail bar with only 8 seats at a single gorgeous wooden counter. Owner Gen Yamamoto, in a white tuxedo, serves a set course of 4-7 cocktails using hyper-seasonal Japanese ingredients. No menu, no music -- just the sound of muddling ice and pouring drinks. Pure minimalist elegance.
howToFind: Located in a quiet residential building in Azabu-Juban. Look for the small, discreet entrance at street level. The bar is tiny and easy to miss.
tips: Reservation essential -- book well in advance. 4-cocktail course around 4400 yen, 7-cocktail course around 7700 yen. No photos of the bar interior. Arrive on time.

name: Roku Nana
description: A hidden rooftop cocktail bar perched atop an apartment building in a Roppongi back alley. Calm, cozy, and sophisticated speakeasy-style experience with open-air Tokyo skyline views. Far from the typical Roppongi chaos.
howToFind: Located in a back alley off the main Roppongi strip. Look for a nondescript apartment building entrance, take the elevator to the top floor. Easy to walk right past it.
tips: Perfect for a quieter evening away from Roppongi's party scene. Great sunset spot. Cocktails are well-crafted and reasonably priced for the area.
mapsQuery: Roku Nana rooftop bar Roppongi Tokyo

name: Ginza Music Bar
nameJa: 銀座ミュージックバー
description: A listening bar by DJ Shinichi Osawa and coffee producer Nobuhiro Toriba. Features 3000 vinyl records, impressive Tannoy speakers, and a carefully curated soundtrack. The cocktails are paired with the music selections. A temple for audiophiles in the heart of Ginza.
howToFind: Located in a basement space in Ginza. The entrance is discreet -- look for a small sign or ask at the building entrance. Part of the Toriba Coffee complex.
tips: Cover charge applies. This is a listening bar -- conversation should be quiet. The DJ sets are exceptional. Great for solo visitors who love vinyl.

name: Record Bar Analog
nameJa: レコードバー アナログ
description: A plush listening bar hidden in an unassuming Shibuya building with the most comfortable seats of any listening bar in Tokyo. Extensive vinyl collection spanning classic rock, jazz, indie, electronic, hip-hop. More staff than typical listening bars, ensuring attentive service.
howToFind: In a nondescript building in Shibuya -- look for a small sign. The interior is a revelation compared to the building exterior.
tips: The plush seating makes this ideal for a long evening session. Order the house cocktails and let the staff curate the music. Good for dates.

name: Grandfather's
nameJa: グランドファーザーズ
description: A 40-year-old listening bar institution. Dimly lit with an extensive record collection spanning decades and genres -- yacht rock, jazz, soul, contemporary pop. The kind of place where time stops and the vinyl keeps spinning.
howToFind: Tucked away in the Jingumae area near Harajuku. The entrance is small and the bar has been in the same location for four decades. Ask locals if you get lost.
tips: Go during weeknights for the most intimate experience. The bartender often takes requests if you ask politely. Cash preferred.

name: Jazz Inn Uncle Tom
nameJa: ジャズイン アンクルトム
description: Established in 1977, one of Tokyo's most cherished jazz listening institutions with over 3000 jazz records. A pilgrimage site for serious jazz lovers. Intimate, smoky atmosphere with exceptional sound system.
howToFind: Located in Kichijoji, a short walk from the station. Look for a small basement-level entrance. The neighborhood is full of music spots but Uncle Tom is the original.
tips: Come with patience and open ears. The owner curates the listening experience. Cover charge includes a drink. Best experienced alone or with one companion.
mapsQuery: Jazz Inn Uncle Tom Kichijoji Tokyo

name: Garageville
description: A listening bar with a selection covering jazz, world music, classic rock and everything in between. Unique for also offering about 20 kinds of craft brews from European, Asian, and rare Japanese microbreweries alongside the vinyl experience.
howToFind: In the backstreets of Shimokitazawa, near the vintage shop area. Small entrance that is easy to miss.
tips: Try the rare Japanese craft beers you cannot find elsewhere. The vinyl selection is eclectic and the owner is passionate about sharing discoveries. Great Shimokitazawa evening stop.

name: Flaneur
description: Disguised as an old-school tobacco shop on Shibuya's Hyakkendana shopping street. Step inside what looks like a vintage tobacconist and discover a cozy, intimate curry house. The contrast between exterior and interior is pure Tokyo magic.
howToFind: On Hyakkendana (Hundred Shops) street in Shibuya. Look for what appears to be a tobacco shop storefront. Push through the entrance to find the curry restaurant inside.
tips: The curry is excellent and affordable. Small seating capacity so there may be a wait during lunch. Cash recommended.

name: Ginza Yoshizawa
description: Tucked away in a basement floor near Ginza-Itchome Station. An exclusive retreat atmosphere with a light wood counter creating an elegant kaiseki setting. The kind of place Tokyo business people keep to themselves.
howToFind: 2 minutes from Ginza-Itchome Station, in the basement of a nondescript building. Look for a small sign near the building entrance and take the stairs down.
tips: Reservation strongly recommended. The counter seats offer the best experience -- watch the chef work. Lunch sets are excellent value compared to dinner.

name: Yakitori Ton Ton
description: Hidden in plain sight under the train tracks near Tokyo Station. A tiny yakitori joint that locals pack into after work. The smoke, the sizzle, and the train rumble overhead create an unforgettable atmosphere.
howToFind: Tucked under the elevated train tracks near Tokyo Station's Yaesu side. Walk along the tracks and look for the small, smoke-filled entrance among the girders.
tips: Go early (5-6pm) to snag a seat. Order the tare (sauce) yakitori and a cold Asahi. This is old Tokyo at its finest. Cash only.
mapsQuery: Yakitori Ton Ton Tokyo Station under tracks

name: Sabouru
description: A retro kissaten (coffee shop) operating since 1955 in the heart of book town. Dark wood interior, stained glass, and an atmosphere frozen in the Showa era. Famous among Jimbocho's booksellers and intellectuals for decades. Their Napolitan spaghetti and cream soda are legendary.
howToFind: On the main Jimbocho book street, look for the distinctive wooden facade with a mountain lodge aesthetic. There are actually two Sabouru shops -- Sabouru and Sabouru 2 (which serves food).
tips: Sabouru 2 next door serves meals including their famous thick-cut sandwich. The original Sabouru is drinks only. Both are tiny -- expect a short wait. Cash only.

name: Kayaba Coffee
description: A beloved Yanaka landmark in a wooden building from 1916, renovated and reopened in 2009 while retaining its Showa-era character. Ground floor is a kissaten, upstairs is a tatami room. Famous for their egg sandwich and Russian coffee (coffee with whipped cream).
howToFind: Near the intersection of Yanaka and Nezu, on a corner. The distinctive old wooden building stands out among the surrounding structures. A 5-minute walk from Nezu Station.
tips: Weekends get very busy -- go early morning for the best experience. The tatami upstairs is special. Try the tamago (egg) sandwich, a local legend.

name: Flamingo
description: A local legend in Shimokitazawa's vintage scene. Curated mix of vintage American denim, retro dresses, leather jackets, and accessories. Everything is clean, well-selected, and Instagram-ready. The gold standard of Tokyo vintage shopping.
howToFind: On one of the main shopping streets in Shimokitazawa, a short walk from the south exit. The distinctive pink flamingo branding is hard to miss once you find the right street.
tips: Prices are fair for the quality of curation. Check the jacket section for standout finds. Multiple locations in Tokyo but Shimokitazawa is the original.

name: Stick Out
description: Every single item in the store is priced at just 800 yen (about $5). A treasure hunt where persistence pays off. The selection rotates constantly, and dedicated thrifters find designer pieces at this flat rate.
howToFind: In the heart of Shimokitazawa's vintage shop cluster, south side of the station. Small storefront packed floor to ceiling.
tips: Visit multiple times if you can -- stock changes daily. Dig through everything, including the back racks. At 800 yen per item, you can afford to take risks on unusual pieces.
mapsQuery: Stick Out vintage Shimokitazawa Tokyo 800 yen

name: KINJI
description: A massive thrift store beloved for its huge selection of trendy items. Prices range from 2000-5000 yen. Multiple floors of clothing organized by type. Popular with Tokyo's fashion-forward youth. Also has a Shimokitazawa location.
howToFind: On Takeshita-dori's side streets in Harajuku. The Harajuku location is the flagship. Look for the large KINJI signage.
tips: The Harajuku location tends to have trendier pieces; Shimokitazawa has more vintage character. Go early on weekdays to avoid crowds. The accessory section is underrated.

name: Kuroneko Marin
description: A beloved Koenji vintage store near Koenji Hikawa Shrine with curated racks of Japanese streetwear, handmade pieces, and one-of-a-kind finds. The owner has an incredible eye for unique pieces that reflect Koenji's punk-meets-artsy character.
howToFind: Near Koenji Hikawa Shrine, on the quieter side streets north of the station. Small storefront with a distinctive cat-themed (kuroneko means black cat) aesthetic.
tips: Chat with the owner if you can -- they know Koenji's vintage scene inside out and can point you to other hidden shops. Prices are very reasonable.

name: Furugiya SANGO
description: A maze of 70s, 80s, and early 2000s fashion with jackets, dresses, and accessories stacked high. The chaotic, treasure-hunt energy is quintessential Koenji. You never know what you will find buried in the piles.
howToFind: On the south side of Koenji Station in the main vintage shopping area. The packed storefront with clothes spilling out is a giveaway.
tips: Set aside at least 30 minutes to dig through everything. The deeper you go, the better the finds. Great for 80s and 90s Japanese fashion pieces.

name: Notime Shimokitazawa
nameJa: ノータイム 下北沢
description: Opened April 2025, a cozy reseller with a classic thrift boutique feel but with a futuristic twist -- it stays open 24 hours. Perfect for late-night thrift runs after the bars or early morning treasure hunting before the crowds.
howToFind: A 3-minute walk from Shimokitazawa Station. Look for the modern storefront that is lit up even in the middle of the night.
tips: The sweet spot is late night (after midnight) when you have the whole place to yourself. New stock appears throughout the day.

name: Jet Set Records
nameJa: ジェットセットレコード
description: One of Tokyo's largest and most popular vinyl stores with a vast selection spanning hip-hop, house, jazz, soul, and more. Both domestic Japanese pressings and international imports. A pilgrimage site for crate diggers worldwide.
howToFind: Near Shimokitazawa Station on the main shopping street. The large storefront with vinyl displayed in the windows is easy to spot.
tips: Check the new arrivals section first. Japanese pressings are often superior quality. Staff are knowledgeable and can recommend based on your taste. Listening stations available.

name: Ella Records
description: A warm, wood-interior vinyl shop known for its diverse selection including Japanese classics, jazz, and rock. Relocated from Setagaya in 2016. The kind of shop where you walk in for 20 minutes and leave 2 hours later with a stack of records.
howToFind: In a side street in Shibuya. The warm wooden interior is visible through the windows. Smaller than the mega-shops but far more curated.
tips: The Japanese pressing section is exceptional. Ask the staff about their picks -- they are passionate and helpful. Prices are fair for the quality.

name: Big Love Records
description: Since 2008, a vinyl and cassette tape haven for indie music fans, tucked down an alley just far enough from Harajuku's busiest streets. Carries indie bands from the US, UK, and Europe that you will not find at larger shops. Also stocks zines and art prints.
howToFind: Down an alley off the main Harajuku streets, past Cat Street area. Small second-floor shop -- look for the stairs with music posters.
tips: If you love indie/alternative music, this is your spot. The cassette tape selection is outstanding. Check their social media for in-store events and release parties.

name: Flash Disc Ranch
nameJa: フラッシュ ディスク ランチ
description: Known for its lively atmosphere, vintage sound system playing records in-store, and a budget-friendly 'three discs for 2000 yen' section. Eclectic selection from funk to Japanese city pop. The in-store sound system demonstration is worth the visit alone.
howToFind: In the heart of Shimokitazawa's shop district. Listen for the music spilling out of the entrance.
tips: The 3-for-2000-yen bin is a goldmine if you dig patiently. Great for discovering Japanese artists you have never heard of. The staff play incredible selections.

name: Next Records
description: Specializes in foreign records with a massive collection of around 10,000 titles primarily from the US and Europe. Focus on 12-inch singles including hip-hop and R&B. Headphone listening stations let you preview before purchasing.
howToFind: In the Shibuya record shop district, near Udagawacho. Look for the densely packed storefront with 12-inch singles displayed prominently.
tips: Use the listening stations -- the staff encourage it. The hip-hop 12-inch selection is among the best in Tokyo. Prices vary but deals can be found in the bins.

name: BASE Record Shop
description: Small but incredibly well-curated store focusing on hardcore and punk records. If you are into the Koenji punk scene, this is ground zero. Japanese punk and hardcore pressings that are nearly impossible to find elsewhere.
howToFind: South side of Koenji Station in the cluster of alternative shops. Tiny storefront but packed with punk and hardcore vinyl.
tips: Ask about Japanese hardcore exclusives. The owner knows every band in the Koenji scene. Combine with visits to Record Boy and Uptown Record Store nearby.
mapsQuery: BASE record shop Koenji punk Tokyo

name: Bohemian's Guild
nameJa: ボヘミアンズ・ギルド
description: A Jimbocho staple since 2004 specializing in unconventional and avant-garde art books. First floor has Western literature, photography, and art. Upstairs features curated paintings, rare books, and handwritten manuscripts. A treasure trove for bibliophiles and art lovers.
howToFind: On the main Jimbocho book street (Yasukuni-dori). Look for the distinctive storefront with art books displayed in the windows. Second floor is the real gem.
tips: Go upstairs for the rare manuscripts and paintings -- most visitors miss the second floor. Prices range from affordable paperbacks to serious collector pieces. English books available.

name: Kitazawa Bookstore
description: Specializes in foreign-language books related to humanities, particularly English and American literature and art. One of Jimbocho's oldest foreign book dealers. The kind of shop where you find first editions of books you did not know existed.
howToFind: On the main Jimbocho strip among the other bookstores. English signage makes it easy to identify among the Japanese-language shops.
tips: Great for finding English-language books about Japan at reasonable prices. The art section has rare finds. Staff speak some English.

name: Magnif
description: A paradise for magazine enthusiasts offering a mix of Western fashion magazines like Vogue alongside Japanese gems like 90s Popeye and Brutus issues. Perfectly preserved vintage magazines that document decades of culture and design.
howToFind: Small storefront on the Jimbocho strip. The window display of colorful vintage magazine covers is the giveaway.
tips: Vintage Japanese fashion and culture magazines from the 80s-90s make incredible souvenirs and design inspiration. The Popeye back issues are especially sought-after. Prices are very fair.

name: Yumeno Shoten
description: A manga specialty store dealing in out-of-print manga and special collections. If you are hunting for a rare manga volume or want to discover obscure titles, this is the place. First editions and complete sets of classic series.
howToFind: Among the Jimbocho bookstores. The manga covers in the window and the slightly otaku aesthetic distinguish it from the literary bookshops nearby.
tips: Bring a list of specific titles you are looking for -- the staff can check their inventory. Prices for rare volumes can be high but are generally fair for the collector market.
mapsQuery: Yumeno Shoten manga bookstore Jimbocho Tokyo

name: Daikanyama T-Site
description: Three interlinked buildings designed as 'A Library in the Woods' by Klein Dytham Architects. Six book departments, extensive English-language magazine selection, vinyl records, and the serene Anjin Lounge upstairs with rare vintage magazines, leather chairs, and live piano. Open until 2am. A cultural destination, not just a bookstore.
howToFind: 5-minute walk from Daikanyama Station (Tokyu-Toyoko Line), or 15-minute walk from Shibuya, 10 minutes from Ebisu. The tree-lined complex is visible from the main road.
tips: Visit the Anjin Lounge on the second floor for cocktails surrounded by rare vintage magazines. The Magazine Street section has international publications. Open 7am-2am. Combine with exploring Daikanyama's boutiques.

name: Mogami Kogei (Edo Sashimono Workshop)
description: A third-generation Edo Sashimono woodworking workshop where Yutaka Mogami, one of the last masters of this nail-free joinery technique, teaches visitors to make chopsticks. He has been practicing for 48 years. A living connection to Edo-period craftsmanship.
howToFind: In the Taito ward workshop district. Booking required through craft experience platforms. The workshop is in a traditional wooden building.
tips: Book well in advance as sessions are limited. The chopstick-making workshop takes about 90 minutes. You keep your handmade chopsticks. Basic Japanese helps but gestures work too.
mapsQuery: Mogami Kogei Edo Sashimono workshop Tokyo

name: Sokichi Edo Kiriko
description: A glass-cutting workshop and shop selling over 1000 types of Edo Kiriko glassware. You can participate in an authentic glass-cutting experience using the same machines and blades as professional artisans, choosing from various glass types, colors, and patterns dating back to 1834.
howToFind: In the Sumida ward area near Kinshicho. The shop displays its stunning cut-glass pieces in the window. Booking required for workshop.
tips: The workshop takes about 90 minutes. You create a unique drinking glass to take home. Choose geometric patterns for easier first attempts. The finished pieces are stunning.
mapsQuery: Sokichi Edo Kiriko glass cutting workshop Tokyo

name: Nisshin Kikinzoku Silver Workshop
description: A 12th-generation silversmith workshop in trendy Kuramae where master craftsman Sohaku Kamikawa guides you through shaping your own bangle from 99.9% pure silver. Practice hammering on copper before creating your final piece. Twelve generations of metalworking mastery.
howToFind: In Kuramae, Tokyo's artisan/maker district along the Sumida River. The workshop is in a traditional building among Kuramae's craft shops and cafes.
tips: Book through their website. The experience takes about 2 hours. Combine with exploring Kuramae's many craft shops and coffee roasters. Your silver bangle is completely unique.
mapsQuery: Nisshin Kikinzoku silver workshop Kuramae Tokyo

name: Nezu Shrine
description: Often called 'Tokyo's Fushimi Inari' for its stunning tunnel of vermillion torii gates, but without the Kyoto crowds. Over 1900 years old according to legend. Hosts the beautiful Bunkyo Azalea Festival in spring with 3000 azalea bushes. One of Tokyo's most photogenic yet uncrowded shrines.
howToFind: A 5-minute walk from Nezu Station (Chiyoda Line). The main entrance with its large torii gate is visible from the street. Head to the back of the grounds for the famous torii tunnel.
tips: Visit early morning for the torii gate tunnel without other visitors. Free entry. The azalea garden in late April is spectacular (small fee for the garden during festival). Combine with a Yanaka walk.
mapsQuery: Nezu Shrine Bunkyo Tokyo torii gates

name: Hakusan Shrine
description: Established in the 10th century and named after one of Japan's most sacred mountains. A secret spot near Tokyo University known primarily to local residents. Especially worth visiting during the hydrangea festival in June, but beautiful year-round.
howToFind: A short walk from Hakusan Station on the Toei Mita Line. The shrine is in a quiet residential area near Tokyo University, far from tourist routes.
tips: The hydrangea festival (Bunkyo Ajisai Matsuri) in June is the highlight but the shrine is peaceful any time. Free admission. Very few tourists. Combine with a walk to nearby Koishikawa Korakuen Garden.

name: Kyu-Shiba-rikyu Gardens
description: A pocket-sized Edo-period landscape garden near Hamamatsucho Station with a central pond surrounded by meticulously maintained grounds. Remarkably uncrowded despite being next to Tokyo Tower and visible from the JR platform. One of Tokyo's oldest gardens, often overlooked for nearby Hamarikyu.
howToFind: Directly adjacent to Hamamatsucho Station's north exit. Literally visible from the JR platform but most commuters walk right past it. Entrance is on the street level.
tips: 150 yen entrance fee. Perfect for a 30-minute contemplative break between train connections. Visit during plum blossom season (late February) or autumn leaves. Uncrowded even on weekends.

name: Nezu Museum Garden
description: A vast, lush forest garden with ponds, tea houses, and winding paths hidden behind the Nezu Museum in the heart of Omotesando. Only accessible with museum admission, ensuring constant tranquility. Feels like stepping into a mountain forest while surrounded by Aoyama's high-end boutiques.
howToFind: Enter through the Nezu Museum on Omotesando's backstreet (Minami-Aoyama). The garden is behind the museum building. Take the path that leads down from the gallery exits.
tips: 1300 yen museum admission includes garden access. The garden alone is worth the price. Multiple tea houses dot the paths. Visit in autumn for spectacular maple colors. Allow 45 minutes for the garden.

name: Institute for Nature Study (Shizen Kyoiku-en)
nameJa: 国立科学博物館附属自然教育園
description: A 20-hectare nature preserve in upscale Minato ward showing Tokyo as it existed before urbanization. Walking paths through natural deciduous forest, wetlands, and meadows with over 200 plant species and numerous birds. Daily visitor cap keeps it uncrowded. A secret known mainly to local naturalists.
howToFind: Near Meguro Station, adjacent to the Tokyo Metropolitan Teien Art Museum. The entrance is easy to miss as it looks like a wall of forest from the street.
tips: 320 yen admission. Daily visitor limit of 300 people keeps it peaceful -- arrive early on weekends. No food or drink inside. Allow 60-90 minutes for the full walking route. Feels like leaving Tokyo entirely.
mapsQuery: Institute for Nature Study Shizen Kyoiku-en Meguro Tokyo

name: GINZA SIX Rooftop Garden
description: An enormous free rooftop garden atop the GINZA SIX department store offering 360-degree views over Ginza and central Tokyo. Seating areas between trees and bushes, perfect for a picnic. Especially magical at night when the city is illuminated. Most tourists never make it to the roof.
howToFind: Take the elevator to the rooftop floor of GINZA SIX department store. The garden is open access during store hours. Entrance is free.
tips: Go at sunset for the best experience. Bring drinks and snacks from the depachika (basement food hall) below. Free entry. One of the best free views in Ginza. Check seasonal hours.

name: Meguro Sky Garden
description: A peaceful rooftop garden built on the 9th floor directly above a highway junction. A bizarre and beautiful Tokyo contradiction -- a tranquil garden floating above roaring traffic. Wide open sky views and a spiral walking path.
howToFind: Above the Ohashi Junction on the Metropolitan Expressway. Enter through the Cross Air Tower building near Ikejiri-Ohashi Station (Denentoshi Line). Take the elevator to the 9th floor.
tips: Free entry. The spiral path gives different perspectives of the city. Particularly atmospheric on cloudy days when the garden feels suspended in the sky. Combine with a walk to Nakameguro.

name: Shin-Marunouchi Building Terrace
description: A free 7th-floor rooftop terrace just steps from Tokyo Station's Marunouchi Exit offering relaxing views of the iconic red-brick station building, the Imperial Palace area, and the Marunouchi business district. Most visitors to Tokyo Station never look up.
howToFind: Enter the Shin-Marunouchi Building (new Marunouchi Building) directly across from Tokyo Station's Marunouchi Exit. Take the elevator to the 7th floor terrace.
tips: Free access. Perfect for photographing Tokyo Station from above. The terrace restaurants are good for a meal with a view. Great night view of the illuminated station.

name: Ginza Mitsukoshi Rooftop Shrine
nameJa: 銀座三越 屋上庭園
description: A hidden rooftop garden and Shinto shrine on the 9th floor of the historic Mitsukoshi department store. A secret oasis above the Ginza crowds with a small shrine, garden, and benches. The juxtaposition of a traditional shrine atop a luxury department store is quintessentially Tokyo.
howToFind: Take the elevator to the 9th floor of Ginza Mitsukoshi. The rooftop garden and shrine are accessible during store hours. Most shoppers have no idea it exists.
tips: Free access. A peaceful escape from Ginza's busy streets below. The shrine is a proper Shinto shrine with an offering box. Combine with exploring the depachika basement food hall.
mapsQuery: Ginza Mitsukoshi rooftop garden shrine 9th floor

name: Meguro Parasitological Museum
description: The world's only museum dedicated entirely to parasites. Founded in 1953, it houses over 60,000 specimens including an 8.8-meter tapeworm extracted from a human host. Free admission. Bizarrely fascinating and a perfect example of Tokyo's embrace of niche obsessions.
howToFind: A 10-minute walk from Meguro Station along Meguro-dori. The museum is in a small, easy-to-miss building. Look for the sign on the left side of the street heading south.
tips: Free admission but donations appreciated. Small gift shop sells parasite-themed merchandise including T-shirts. Takes about 30-45 minutes. Not for the squeamish. Combine with nearby Meguro restaurants.

name: Fukagawa Edo Museum
description: A full-scale recreation of an Edo-period neighborhood inside a massive atrium. Walk through life-sized homes, shops, and even a canal. The lighting changes to simulate time of day. You can rent a kimono and explore in period style. Occasional live shamisen performances.
howToFind: A 5-minute walk from Kiyosumi-Shirakawa Station (Hanzomon/Oedo Lines). Follow signs from the station. The museum building is modern from the outside -- the Edo magic is all inside.
tips: 400 yen admission. Allow 60-90 minutes. The lighting changes every 45 minutes simulating dawn to dusk -- time your visit to see the transition. Combine with Kiyosumi Garden next door.

name: Intermediatheque
nameJa: インターメディアテク
description: One of Tokyo's few free museums, housed in the beautifully restored former Tokyo Central Post Office building. Displays academic collections from the University of Tokyo including zoological specimens, minerals, antique scientific instruments, and occasionally creepy taxidermy. A cabinet of curiosities aesthetic.
howToFind: Inside the KITTE building directly connected to Tokyo Station's Marunouchi South Exit. Enter KITTE and go to the 2nd and 3rd floors. Free admission.
tips: Free admission. No photography allowed in most areas. The mix of Victorian-style display cases with modern architecture is stunning. Allow 45-60 minutes. Combine with the KITTE rooftop for Tokyo Station views.

name: Yanaka Ginza Shopping Street
description: A 170-meter lantern-lined retro shopping street with about 60 shops that survived wars and earthquakes intact. Walking through feels like time-traveling to the Showa era. Famous for its stray cats, croquettes, and old-school Tokyo atmosphere. Start at Yuyake Dandan (Sunset Steps) for the full experience.
howToFind: Walk from Nippori Station's west exit, through the Yanaka cemetery, and descend the famous Yuyake Dandan steps. The shopping street begins at the bottom of the stairs.
tips: Visit at sunset -- the Yuyake Dandan steps face west and the golden light is magical. Try the menchi-katsu (fried meat patty) and cat-tail shaped donuts. Most shops close by 7pm. Cat spotting is a local sport.
mapsQuery: Yanaka Ginza shopping street Nippori Tokyo

name: Togoshi Ginza
description: Tokyo's longest open-air shotengai at 1.3km with around 400 stores. Famous for its street food, especially the Togoshi croquette in flavors from classic beef to curry and cheese. A friendly, laid-back local shopping street completely off the tourist radar.
howToFind: Togoshi-Ginza Station on the Tokyu Ikegami Line. The shotengai begins right at the station exit and stretches in both directions.
tips: Come hungry -- the street food is the main attraction. Try croquettes from multiple shops and compare. Weekday afternoons have the most local energy. Virtually zero tourists.
mapsQuery: Togoshi Ginza shotengai shopping street Tokyo

name: Sugamo Jizo-dori
description: Known as 'Grandma's Harajuku' -- a peaceful shopping street catering to Tokyo's older generation with 200+ shops. Red underwear shops (for good luck), traditional sweets, and an atmosphere that is the anti-Shibuya. The Togenuki Jizo temple at its center is believed to heal ailments.
howToFind: From Sugamo Station (JR Yamanote Line), take the north exit. The shotengai begins immediately. The Togenuki Jizo temple is about midway down the street.
tips: Visit on the 4th, 14th, or 24th of the month for the ennichi (festival market) with extra street vendors. Buy red underwear as a lucky souvenir. The shio-daifuku (salt mochi) from the famous shop is a must-try.

name: Nakano Broadway
description: A five-floor complex that draws Tokyo's otaku community with second-hand manga, anime DVDs, vintage toys, action figures, and rare collectibles. More authentic and less tourist-oriented than Akihabara. The Mandarake shops scattered throughout are legendary for rare finds.
howToFind: 5-minute walk from Nakano Station's north exit. Walk through the covered Nakano Sun Mall shopping arcade -- it leads directly to Broadway's entrance.
tips: Multiple Mandarake specialty shops on different floors focus on different genres. The upper floors are the most interesting. Bring cash for small vendors. Way less crowded than Akihabara with better finds.

name: 20000 Den-Atsu
description: The reincarnation of legendary Koenji venue 20000 Volt, established as a premier destination for punk, noise, and hardcore. Live shows almost every night in a raw, sweaty basement space. The beating heart of Koenji's punk scene.
howToFind: South side of Koenji Station. In the backstreets among bars and vintage shops. Look for show flyers and listen for the sound check.
tips: Check their schedule online for upcoming shows. Cover charges typically 2000-3000 yen including a drink. Bring earplugs. Shows start early (often 6-7pm). The crowd is passionate and welcoming to foreigners.

name: Koenji High
description: A modern live house with state-of-the-art sound and lighting that opened in 2008. Shows almost every night showcasing a vibrant mix of genres from punk to electronic to experimental. Koenji's punk heritage meets 21st century production quality.
howToFind: Near Koenji Station's south exit. Slightly larger and more visible than other Koenji venues. Check their website for the schedule and door times.
tips: Buy tickets in advance for popular acts through their website or at the door. Sound quality is excellent for the venue size. Mix of Japanese and international acts.

name: Shinjuku Pit Inn
description: Near or at the top of any list of live jazz venues in Tokyo. Operating for decades in Shinjuku, it hosts Japan's top jazz musicians and international acts in an intimate basement setting. The afternoon matinee shows are a Tokyo jazz institution.
howToFind: In Shinjuku 2-chome area near Shinjuku-Sanchome Station. Basement level with stairs down from street level. Look for the iconic sign.
tips: Afternoon shows (2:30pm) are cheaper (1300 yen) than evening shows (3000+ yen). Evening shows are the main event with bigger acts. No talking during performances -- this is serious jazz listening.

name: Miyazaki Clock at Nittele Tower
description: A giant mechanical fantasy clock designed by Studio Ghibli's Hayao Miyazaki standing 10 meters high and 18 meters wide on the Nittele Tower. Performs a spectacular mechanical show at scheduled times with moving parts, steam, and music. Hidden in plain sight -- most tourists walk right past.
howToFind: On the exterior of Nittele (Nippon Television) Tower in Shiodome, a short walk from Shimbashi Station. The clock is on the building's street-level facade.
tips: Check performance times -- it activates at noon, 3pm, and 6pm (schedules vary). The mechanical performance lasts about 3 minutes. Free to watch. Best viewed from directly in front of the building.
mapsQuery: Miyazaki Ghibli clock Nittele Tower Shiodome Tokyo

name: Kyu Asakura House
description: A beautifully preserved traditional wooden residence from 1919, once home to a Tokyo Prefectural Assembly councilor. Tatami rooms with sliding screens look out over a hidden Japanese garden. A tranquil time capsule steps from trendy Daikanyama's boutiques.
howToFind: A 2-minute walk from Daikanyama Station. On a quiet side street near T-Site. The wooden entrance gate is easy to miss -- look for it on the left side of the hill road near Hillside Terrace.
tips: 100 yen admission. Open 10am-6pm, closed Mondays. The garden is particularly beautiful in autumn. Sit on the engawa (wooden veranda) and contemplate the garden. Combine with T-Site visit.

name: Tower Records Shibuya
nameJa: タワーレコード渋谷店
description: A nine-story monument to music culture and the world's largest Tower Records. The 6th floor is dedicated to vinyl with both new releases and vintage finds. In an era where Tower Records died everywhere else, Shibuya's flagship thrives as a cultural institution. The rooftop occasionally hosts live events.
howToFind: On the main road in Shibuya (Fire-dori/Koen-dori area), impossible to miss with its massive yellow signage. A 5-minute walk from Shibuya Station's Hachiko exit.
tips: The 6th floor vinyl section is the destination. Check the Japanese pressing exclusives. The listening booths let you try before you buy. Check the event board for in-store live performances.
